British and American words versus FITASC

Many coaches you will work with grew up with English Sporting, run in England by the CPSA, or with American Sporting Clays under the NSCA. Their words are close to FITASC words, but the rules behind them differ. The biggest difference is the gun position.

Under NSCA rules, and in English Sporting as it is commonly shot, a shooter may start “gun up”, with the gun already mounted before the call. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ that is not allowed. In the ready position the stock stays below the line on the vest until the target appears, and each target is shot from the shoulder. In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free, as under NSCA rules. So “pre-mount this one” is a training drill, but at a Sporting™ competition it earns a yellow card (Chapter 12 · Yellow card for gun position). Translate it, and if the guest is about to compete, ask the coach whether to mention the rule.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 3 · When the gun may be mounted

Pairs have different names. A “true pair” (British and American) is a FITASC simultaneous double: both targets leave at the same time. A “report pair” is a double on report: the second target is launched by the sound of your first shot. A “following pair” is a FITASC rafale: two targets from the same trap, one right after the other. A “show pair” is the presentation of a pair before shooting. A “peg” is the shooting stand, “station” is the American word for a stand, and a “cage” is the frame around it.

Results talk differs too. “HOA”, High Over All, is the overall winner. Classes such as AA, A, B or C are national skill levels, set from a shooter’s registered scores. They are not FITASC age categories, and not the FITASC difficulty classes A, B and C, which rate how hard a trajectory is.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Allowed: the shooter has two cartridges for the double and may fire both at the same target.

Compak® Sporting

Not allowed: one cartridge per target, and firing both at the first target is prohibited.

So even within FITASC the same words can carry different rules. Ask yourself each time which rulebook the speaker has in mind.

Key points

  • Gun up: allowed under NSCA rules and common in English Sporting; not allowed in FITASC Sporting™; free in Compak® Sporting
  • True pair = simultaneous; report pair = on report; following pair = rafale
  • Peg = shooting spot; station = stand (US); cage = protective frame
  • HOA = overall winner; AA/A/B/C classes are not FITASC categories or difficulty classes
  • Sporting™: both shots at one target allowed; Compak® Sporting: one per target
Stand Talk

  • Coach Pre-mount this one for now.

    Meaning: Training drill: start with the gun in the shoulder. Not allowed in FITASC Sporting™ competition.

  • Coach It’s a true pair.

    Meaning: Both targets leave at the same time (FITASC: simultaneous double).

  • Coach Following pair off the left trap.

    Meaning: Two targets from the same trap one after the other (FITASC: rafale).

  • Coach Let’s see a show pair.

    Meaning: Throw the pair once so everyone can watch it before shooting.

  • Coach He’s AA class and won HOA last year.

    Meaning: A high national skill class, and overall winner of the event.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. A British coach says “It’s a true pair.” What is the FITASC term?

    1. A double on report
    2. A rafale double
    3. A simultaneous double
    4. A correct double
    Answer

    A simultaneous double

    “True pair” is the British and American name for two targets released together, a FITASC simultaneous double.

    Chapter 4 · Simultaneous double

  2. In which discipline is a “gun up” start NOT allowed?

    1. Sporting™
    2. Compak® Sporting (FITASC)
    3. English Sporting (CPSA)
    4. Sporting Clays (NSCA)
    Answer

    Sporting™

    Sporting™ requires the stock below the vest line until the target appears. Compak® Sporting leaves the gun position free, and so do NSCA rules and English Sporting as commonly shot.

    Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun

  3. A guest reads “Class C” in British results. What is it?

    1. A FITASC age category
    2. A national skill level set by scores
    3. The hardest FITASC trajectory class
    4. A type of cartridge
    Answer

    A national skill level set by scores

    In British and American results classes are skill levels. FITASC uses A, B and C only for trajectory difficulty and has age categories for people.
